extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, reporters, newsroom editors, and media studies students
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the procedural rituals reporters use to claim 'objectivity' and how those rituals function as newsworthiness and selection criteria in newsroom practice. Useful for analyzing how news is produced and why some events are covered while others are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes of the story exemplifying news procedures (e.g., quotation marks, conflict-of-views structure, supporting evidence sequencing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories are judged 'objective' if they display recognizable professional forms — e.g., use of direct quotes, presentation of opposing views, and a sequencing of evidence that mirrors accepted news practice. These formal markers signal that reporting followed routine procedures rather than personal whim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Notions of social reality the newsman takes for granted; which institutions are presumed legitimate, which sources presumed reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content is evaluated against reporters' and organizations' tacit assumptions about legitimacy: whether actors are authoritative, institutions are credible, and social facts are accepted. Material incompatible with those taken-for-granted assumptions is less likely to pass as 'objective' news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-organizational relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter's experience with regular sources/beats shapes what is treated as factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reporter's routine interactions with institutions and official sources (e.g., police, government offices) influence which events can be credibly reported; established relationships make it easier to obtain quotable, on-the-record sources and documentation that satisfy objectivity rituals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of conflicting possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: When a fact is contested, present 'both sides.' Reporting one source's claim against another's claim insulates the reporter from accusations of bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showcasing competing claims or perspectives functions as a defensive technique: by attributing each claim to a source rather than asserting a reporter's judgment, the reporter avoids responsibility for asserting truth. This ritual makes contested matters appear balanced even when evidence is unequal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Buttress claims with corroborative facts (statistics, dates, documents) so the assertion appears self-evidently true rather than the reporter's opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing corroboration (documents, records, statistics, multiple sources) shifts epistemic weight away from the reporter and toward 'objective' artifacts; the presence and sequencing of such evidence are treated as decisive markers of objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious use of quotation marks / attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing claims to a named source ('the senator said') removes the reporter as author of the assertion. Direct quotes shift epistemic responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using direct attribution and quotation signals that claims originate with identifiable actors; this reduces reporter accountability for contested assertions and is a routine safeguard against accusations such as bias or libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring information in an appropriate sequence (Inverted Pyramid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting the most 'important' facts first signals that selection followed a recognized professional convention rather than a personal whim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhering to conventions like the inverted pyramid communicates that editorial judgment was proceduralized. Sequence and prominence operate as proof that story selection was professional and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural eligibility as newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is more newsworthy if it can be reported through these rituals — i.e., if there is an authoritative source willing to be quoted, if there are clear 'two sides,' if there are documents to cite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness is not only intrinsic to events but contingent on whether they can be processed through objectivity rituals. Editors favor events that readily produce the formal signs of objective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for source-rich events
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with named, on-the-record spokespeople are systematically preferred over stories where evidence requires the reporter to speak in their own voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that supply official spokespeople, documents, or clear opposing claims are advantaged because they permit reporters to attribute claims and avoid making unaided judgments. Lack of accessible authoritative sources reduces a story's chances of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive bias / risk minimization
rubrics_metrics.description: News selection skews toward items that protect the reporter from libel suits and editor questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures labeled 'objectivity' function defensively: they are used to minimize legal and editorial risk. This can bias coverage toward safer, more attributable stories and away from risky investigations or coverage of slow, complex phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual ≠ truth (procedures can suppress judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: These procedures often function to suppress news judgment rather than enable it; following ritual does not guarantee accuracy or completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tuchman emphasizes that adherence to objectivity rituals is not the same as achieving truth; the rituals can exclude important topics and simplify complex realities in ways that make reporting appear objective while omitting substantive truth claims.
